Le choix d'un métier

Le métier constitue un élément essentiel de cette profession.

Dans les règles historiques de référence, le personnage Sans Profession choisit une occupation, qui permet au Meneur de déterminer les compétences considérées comme professionnelles ou courantes en fonction de son activité.

Les exemples comprennent notamment les artisans, les fermiers, les éleveurs, les marchands, les guérisseurs ordinaires, les aubergistes, les artistes et les bateliers.

Dans MERP-UI, ce principe doit être appliqué en respectant les mécanismes effectivement disponibles. Le choix narratif d'un métier ne modifie pas automatiquement les coûts de développement ou les catégories de compétences. Toute adaptation supplémentaire doit relever des règles prévues ou d'une décision explicite du Meneur.

Magie

Le Sans Profession ne possède aucune Liste de sorts de base, aucun royaume privilégié et aucune spécialisation magique professionnelle.

L'apprentissage éventuel de sorts dépend des possibilités générales du système RMU et des restrictions applicables. Aucun accès magique supplémentaire ne doit être déduit du seul choix de la profession.

Profession, métier et culture

Le Sans Profession représente une orientation générale de formation. Son métier précise les connaissances qu'il possède, tandis que sa culture détermine les traditions, les langues et les usages qui ont façonné son existence.

Un fermier rohir, un artisan khazâd et un marchand dorwinadan partagent ainsi la même profession mécanique, tout en possédant des identités profondément différentes.

Il convient enfin de distinguer cette catégorie ludique des personnages décrits par Tolkien. Sam Gamegie, le Fermier Magotte et Prosper Poiredebeurré offrent des inspirations remarquables pour cette profession, mais leur existence littéraire ne doit pas être réduite à une fiche mécanique particulière.

Le Sans Profession prend toute sa dimension lorsque le personnage possède un passé concret, des relations personnelles et des compétences qui ont une véritable utilité dans le monde. L'aventure transforme progressivement son expérience, sans effacer les connaissances et les attachements qui ont donné sa forme à sa vie antérieure.

Layman

The Trades and Everyday Lives of Middle-earth

Autumn is well advanced in the Bree-land. For several days, rain has soaked the roads, and the last wagons laden with the harvest make their way with difficulty towards the villages. Most of the fields have been reaped, the barns are full, and families are laying in the stores that must see them through the winter.

At the end of a narrow lane, behind a whitewashed house, a woman is at work in a carpenter's workshop. Neatly stacked planks occupy part of the yard, while several wagon wheels await repair beneath a lean-to. The smell of freshly cut timber mingles with the smoke from the fire burning in the neighbouring smithy.

The woman's name is Elwen. She is thirty-seven years old and has worked with wood since her adolescence. Her father taught her to distinguish one kind of timber from another, to select pieces dry enough for making a wheel, and to assemble the timbers of a roof. Since his death, she has run the workshop with the help of two apprentices. The farmers of the surrounding countryside know her work, and merchants who regularly pass through Bree readily entrust the repair of their wagons to her.

That morning, a boy came to tell her that a caravan had stopped on the road, a few leagues to the east. One of its wagons had lost a wheel while crossing a particularly muddy stretch. The drivers had hoped to reach Bree before nightfall, but their horses were exhausted, and several sacks of grain were in danger of being spoiled by the rain.

Elwen finishes the task she had begun, gathers a few tools, and tells her apprentice to prepare a replacement wheel. She knows the merchant leading the caravan. Every year he brings provisions intended for the people of the villages, and he has a reputation for being a careful man, little inclined to take needless risks.

An hour later, she reaches the travellers.

The damaged wagon rests beside a ditch, leaning to one side. The drivers have placed stones beneath its axle to prevent it from tipping any farther. Elwen examines the damage, checks the condition of the parts still intact, and establishes that the wheel broke when a piece of timber, already weakened, finally gave way.

She has some of the sacks unloaded, then asks two men to help her raise the wagon. The new wheel can be fitted, but the axle requires a few further repairs. With her tools, she trims the damaged sections and fashions a reinforcing piece that will hold until the wagon reaches her workshop.

As she works, she listens to the merchants' conversation. They speak of a company of travellers met the previous day, and of a bridge whose planks have been carried away by the floods. Farther east, a family is said to have abandoned its farm after discovering troubling tracks near its pastures.

Elwen knows that bridge. She helped repair it some years earlier and remembers an old track that rejoins the road by way of the higher ground. She explains to the drivers how to follow it, then finishes her work.

As she prepares to leave, the caravan master asks whether she would accompany them as far as a village beyond the damaged crossing. Its inhabitants are expecting the grain supplies, and the convoy may have to turn back if the bridge remains impassable. Elwen knows what repairs are needed and might be able to get them across.

She hesitates. Her workshop requires constant attention, several commissions must be delivered before winter, and her young son is waiting for her at home. Yet she also knows the families living on the far side of the hills. One has entrusted work to her for many years, and she understands how serious a delayed delivery can become when the first snows make the roads difficult.

At last, she agrees to go for a few days.

Back in Bree, she prepares her tools, gathers a few changes of clothing, and leaves the urgent work in the hands of her most experienced apprentice. The following morning, she will set out with the merchants.

Elwen has never served in an army, studied under a master of magic, or learned the ways of the Rangers. She knows materials, the customs of trade, the roads of her homeland, and the people living in the neighbouring villages. She can tend a fire, negotiate the price of a commission, treat a minor injury, and recognise the signs of a harsh winter.

Such knowledge has allowed her to build a settled life, raise her child, and earn the respect of those familiar with her work.

For the first time, it will take her beyond the roads she ordinarily travels.

And when she discovers the dangers awaiting the travellers, she will have to rely on the same qualities that have made her a skilled craftswoman: observation, patience, sound judgement, and the determination to fulfil a promise.

In MERP-RMU, a character such as Elwen belongs to the Layman profession.

A Life Before Adventure

Middle-earth is inhabited by peoples whose lives depend upon the daily work of their communities. Great cities, villages, farming estates, and isolated settlements are home to men and women who devote their years to the trades and occupations that sustain those around them.

Farmers till the land and tend their herds. Craftspeople build houses, make tools, and repair the objects upon which ordinary activities depend. Merchants carry goods between regions, while boatmen provide passage across rivers and waterways. In the households of lords, servants, stewards, and scribes contribute to the running of establishments whose responsibilities may be considerable.

The Layman profession represents these characters, whose training does not correspond to any of the major specialisations usually associated with the life of an adventurer.

Its name denotes a category within the game system. Such a character often has a clearly defined occupation, sometimes pursued with exceptional skill. Their apprenticeship has simply followed a different path from that of a Fighter, a Thief, a Ranger, or a spellcaster.

This distinction is particularly important in Middle-earth. Tolkien's tales give an essential place to characters whose lives had seemingly been destined to continue far from the great wars. Their knowledge, loyalty, and attachment to ordinary things can become decisive when they are drawn into events beyond their experience.

The Layman's identity is therefore deeply rooted in their origins. Their occupation, family, culture, and the circumstances of their life are the essential foundations of their training.

Learning the Ways of an Ordinary Life

Most Layman characters acquire their skills from their family, a master, or a community in which knowledge is passed on through practice.

A child raised on a farm gradually becomes familiar with work in the fields, the behaviour of animals, and the changes that accompany the seasons. The child learns to recognise the right time for sowing, to preserve stores of food, and to maintain the tools needed for the harvest.

In a workshop, apprenticeship takes another form. The young craftsperson begins by watching the master's movements, preparing materials, and carrying out the simplest tasks. Over the years, growing precision allows the apprentice to produce work upon which their own reputation will depend.

A merchant's training rests more upon human relations, trade, and knowledge of goods. The apprentice learns to assess the quality of merchandise, keep accounts, negotiate, and understand the customs of the regions visited.

A servant attached to a great household develops other abilities. Such a person knows the habits of their masters, the rules of hospitality, and the duties required to keep a household running. Some become stewards capable of administering substantial stores and directing numerous servants.

These apprenticeships have one thing in common: they unfold over many years, through repeated practice and experience gained alongside others.

The Layman's knowledge thus reflects the demands of their life. Some skills are highly specialised, while others arise from the variety of tasks in which the character has had to take part.

Farms and Cultivated Lands

Rural communities have an important place in Middle-earth. Fields, orchards, and pastures surround the villages, providing the resources needed by their inhabitants and by neighbouring settlements.

A farmer knows the qualities of the soil, the seasons favourable to particular crops, and the signs that herald a change in the weather. The farmer can maintain tools, watch over stores, and recognise difficulties that might endanger a harvest.

Herders possess an intimate knowledge of their animals. They learn to identify common illnesses, prepare pastures, and organise the movement of their herds. In some regions, these responsibilities demand considerable physical endurance and precise knowledge of the paths.

The inhabitants of the Shire provide one of the best-known examples of these traditions. Their lives are closely bound to gardens, cultivated land, meals, and family relationships.

Sam Gamgee, the gardener of Bag End, has practical knowledge of plants and the work needed to tend them. His everyday experience acquires new importance when he accompanies Frodo on his journey. His ability to prepare food, organise the camp's belongings, and endure privation makes a profound contribution to the survival of his companions.

Farmer Maggot, who lives at Bamfurlong in the Marish, offers another example. He knows his land, his animals, and the people who ordinarily cross his property. When a Black Rider comes to question him about Frodo, he stands firm and refuses to be intimidated.

Such figures show how many valuable resources ordinary people possess. Their experience springs from real responsibilities discharged over years within their communities.

Craftspeople and Their Work

Craftspeople hold an essential place in towns and villages alike. Their knowledge makes it possible to build dwellings, manufacture equipment, and maintain the objects upon which other trades depend.

A smith works metal and makes the tools needed in everyday life. Their knowledge encompasses temperatures, the strength of materials, and manufacturing techniques. A smith may also repair weapons and armour without ever having received the training required to use them in battle.

A carpenter knows the different kinds of timber, methods of joining them, and the stresses to which buildings are subjected. Their work ranges from roof structures to furniture, wagons, and certain constructions used in agriculture.

Tailors, weavers, and tanners possess other kinds of expertise. Their work requires an understanding of materials, tools, and techniques handed down by previous generations.

Among the Dwarves, craftsmanship has a particularly important place. The traditions of the various Houses preserve remarkable knowledge of metals, stone, and underground constructions. A Khazâd who devotes their life to making tools or building a hall may attain exceptional mastery of their trade without belonging to a magical or military profession.

The worth of a craftsperson rests upon the quality of their work. Their reputation grows through commissions, completed pieces, and the trust of those who seek their services.

When an adventure begins, this experience remains valuable. A craftsperson may spot a defect in a building, understand how a mechanism works, or identify a material unfamiliar to their companions.

Merchants and the Roads of Trade

Trade has connected the peoples of Middle-earth since ancient times. Roads make it possible to transport agricultural produce, materials, tools, and goods from places that may be very far apart.

A merchant gains particular knowledge of the communities with which they deal. They learn their customs, languages, and the goods they need. Some practise their trade from a shop, while others spend much of the year travelling with caravans.

Their work calls for varied skills. A merchant must appraise merchandise, negotiate prices, organise transport, and keep the records needed to conduct business properly.

Yet the roads are dangerous. Bad weather delays convoys, crossings become impassable, and certain regions remain vulnerable to attack. Experienced merchants learn to choose their routes, safeguard their supplies, and recognise when prudence requires them to change their plans.

The Dorwinrim, who inhabit the fertile lands of Dorwinion, offer a particularly interesting setting for this profession. Their dealings with neighbouring peoples encourage the circulation of goods, languages, and regional knowledge.

In the ports of Gondor, merchant houses have other traditions. River and sea trade demand knowledge of vessels, cargoes, and relations between coastal settlements.

A merchant who joins a company of adventurers brings experience whose value goes well beyond bargaining. Such a character knows how to speak with strangers, judge certain risks, and understand the concerns of the communities through which the company passes.

Boatmen and the People of the Ports

Rivers and seas play a major role in the commerce of Middle-earth. Those who live along their banks know the currents, fords, and places where boats can find shelter.

A boatman learns to handle a vessel, recognise changes in the water level, and carry people and goods through conditions that may be difficult. The work demands constant attention to natural phenomena and a sound knowledge of the waterways travelled.

Ports have a more complex organisation. Cargoes must be unloaded, ships maintained, and merchandise distributed among the warehouses. Harbourmasters, shipwrights, fishermen, and traders all contribute to this daily activity.

In Pelargir, a character may have grown up among the vessels that travel the Anduin. Such a person knows the trades of the quays, the habits of sailors, and the difficulties peculiar to river voyages.

In the northern regions, a boatman of Eriador has different experience, suited to smaller rivers and the crossings that connect communities.

Such characters can become valuable companions when an adventure requires the company to cross a river, examine a vessel, or prepare for a journey by water.

Servants and Stewards

The life of great households depends upon many people whose responsibilities are seldom among the deeds celebrated in stories.

Servants know the habits of those they attend, the customs of hospitality, and the tasks needed to maintain a household. Some prepare meals, while others look after clothing, stores, or the reception of visitors.

Stewards bear wider responsibilities. They organise work, administer resources, and oversee the running of estates entrusted to their care. Their occupation requires social knowledge, a good memory, and sometimes a command of several languages.

In the great cities of Gondor, the residences of noble families and administrative establishments offer many possibilities for such characters. A steward may have spent years managing stores, receiving messengers, and arranging a master's journeys.

Among the Dúnedain of the North, more scattered communities maintain different forms of service. The management of resources, the carrying of messages, and the preservation of family traditions nevertheless remain important.

An understanding of human relationships is often one of these characters' greatest strengths. An experienced servant can recognise tensions within a household, understand what a visitor expects, and maintain the discretion certain duties require.

When such a person leaves familiar surroundings, these qualities may allow them to adapt to situations that more specialised companions would find harder to approach.

The Wisdom of Ordinary Lives

Tolkien's tales place particular importance on characters whose strength lies in qualities developed over the course of a peaceful life.

Hobbits hold a remarkable place in this tradition. Their attachment to family, home, and the simple pleasures of life stands in profound contrast to the ambitions of the powerful.

Sam Gamgee is one of its finest examples. His loyalty to Frodo, his endurance, and his ability to preserve hope in the darkest moments are rooted in a life devoted to gardening, family ties, and everyday responsibilities.

Barliman Butterbur, the innkeeper of the Prancing Pony in Bree, represents another kind of competence. He knows his customers, the travellers passing through the country, and the habits of his community. His concerns are those of a man who must maintain his establishment, welcome strangers, and ensure the safety of his guests.

These characters remind us how deeply human qualities can influence events. Loyalty, prudence, hospitality, and the ability to persevere in a difficult task arise from experiences acquired long before the beginning of an adventure.

The Layman offers a way to portray this essential aspect of Middle-earth: people whose ordinary activities help sustain their communities throughout the long years separating the great events of history.

Defending Oneself When Necessary

Most Layman characters have received no martial training comparable to that of Fighters or Rangers. Nevertheless, the circumstances of their lives may have led them to learn the use of certain weapons.

A farmer may use a spear to protect livestock, while a hunter has experience with a bow. A sailor might have learned to wield a short blade during voyages, and a merchant sometimes accompanies convoys exposed to brigands.

Such knowledge is generally bound to the circumstances of their lives. A craftsperson may be sturdy enough to defend themselves in a brawl yet lack the experience needed to face a trained combatant. An occasional guard knows the basic movements of a shield without possessing the techniques developed by professional soldiers.

The distinction lies in training. The Layman's martial skills arise from particular needs rather than from an apprenticeship devoted chiefly to combat.

When adventure begins, this experience may enable the character to survive a first dangerous encounter. The ordeals that follow then become opportunities to learn from more experienced companions.

Culture as a True Inheritance

The Layman profession leaves a particularly important place for the character's cultural origins.

A Harfoot Hobbit may have grown up in a village of the Shire, among a family deeply attached to cultivated land and local customs. Their knowledge concerns gardens, meals, family relationships, and the paths they have travelled since childhood.

A Rohir raised among the herds possesses an intimate familiarity with horses. Even if not a soldier, riding and tending animals occupy an important place in such a person's life.

A Khazâd may be a craftsperson, merchant, miner, or steward in the service of their House. Family traditions, the study of materials, and obligations towards kin form the foundations of their existence.

A Dorwinadan trained in trade knows the products of their homeland and the relationships between the communities that exchange them. A Gondorian of Minas Tirith may have been trained as a scribe or steward, while someone from the countryside possesses knowledge suited to farming and rural life.

Among the Elves, a character may have devoted many years to craftwork, study, or the upkeep of their people's dwellings. Longevity sometimes allows such a person to acquire considerable experience without having undergone an adventurer's training.

These differences should guide the selection of skills, languages, and areas of knowledge. Culture provides the character's original environment; occupation defines how they have lived within it.

The First Dangers

When the Layman leaves familiar surroundings, the limits of their experience quickly become apparent.

Long marches, nights spent far from inhabited places, and armed confrontations may prove to be ordeals for which nothing has prepared them. A merchant accustomed to well-travelled roads may find themselves at a loss in a region where the paths have vanished. A craftsperson who knows every material used in the workshop may have no idea how to find food in the wild lands.

Such difficulties form an important part of the character's development.

The character learns to prepare a camp, recognise the dangers of a route, and make use of the resources available to the company. They also discover the habits of their companions, some of whom possess experience very different from their own.

Yet the character retains their own skills. When a wheel breaks, an object needs repairing, or a negotiation becomes necessary, that knowledge proves its worth once more.

Adventure thus gradually changes the way the character regards their experience. Actions performed for years in the course of an ordinary trade may become the means of overcoming an unexpected difficulty.

Loyalty and the Temptations of the Shadow

Layman characters often have deep ties to their families, their communities, and the places where they grew up.

These relationships can become a remarkable source of courage. A farmer agrees to cross dangerous country in search of a missing relative; a merchant risks their possessions to bring provisions to an isolated village; a servant remains loyal to someone under threat, although abandoning that person would secure their own safety.

Yet these same attachments can become sources of conflict. The desire to preserve a family business sometimes leads a person to accept dangerous arrangements. Fear of losing one's possessions, jealousy, or ambition may influence the decisions of someone accustomed to a settled life.

The Shadow is eager to exploit such weaknesses. Promises of wealth, power, or safety may tempt those who fear losing what they have built.

The Layman's strength often lies in convictions acquired over a lifetime. Keeping one's word, standing by one's neighbours, and honouring commitments give the character principles to which they may remain faithful when they encounter events beyond their experience.

The profession thus offers many opportunities to portray a character whose moral choices arise from ordinary circumstances before coming face to face with the great threats of Middle-earth.

The Layman Through the Ages

The profession naturally has a place in every Age of Middle-earth, for every people has occupations necessary to its livelihood.

In the First Age, a Layman may belong to human communities established in Beleriand, to the craftspeople of Elven kingdoms, or to the families accompanying the great migrations. The wars against Morgoth overturn their lives, sometimes forcing inhabitants to abandon their lands and embark upon journeys whose dangers they cannot foresee.

In the Second Age, the rise of Númenor provides a particularly rich setting for craftspeople, sailors, merchants, and scholars. Númenórean settlements in Middle-earth encourage exchanges between peoples, while the island's great political transformations gradually affect the lives of its inhabitants. A character may be drawn into these events even though their concerns had until then been confined to their occupation or family.

In the Third Age, the profession takes countless forms. The people of Bree, the farmers of the Shire, the craftspeople of Gondor, the merchants of Dorwinion, and the boatmen of Rhovanion all offer possibilities. The advance of the Shadow and the wars affecting many regions sometimes compel such characters to leave their familiar lives behind.

In the Fourth Age, the restoration of the Reunited Kingdom opens new prospects. Roads are gradually made safe, damaged settlements rebuilt, and trade between peoples renewed. A Layman may take part in this transformation as a craftsperson, merchant, farmer, or administrator. New relationships between kingdoms also offer many reasons to travel.

Each Age thus gives the profession a particular place. The character's occupation, resources, and traditions should reflect the history of the people to which they belong.

When Adventure Begins

For a Layman, setting out often marks a significant break with the life they once knew.

An unexpected event may compel the character to leave home. A caravan has disappeared, a neighbouring community asks for help, or a loved one has failed to return from a journey. A chance discovery may also change the course of their life: a manuscript found in an attic, an ancient object entrusted to them by a traveller, or a message intended for someone they do not know.

Some characters take to the road out of curiosity. A young merchant wishes to discover the regions known only through the products they sell; a craftsperson seeks a master capable of teaching a particular technique; a scholar wants to examine the remains of an ancient settlement.

Others depart after a loss. Their home has been destroyed, their family scattered, or their livelihood ruined by war. The journey then becomes a way of finding a place in the world once more.

Within a company, the Layman brings practical abilities, social knowledge, and experience often very different from that of other adventurers. Their presence is a reminder that not every difficulty can be overcome by combat or magic.

The character's development comes gradually. Journeys build physical endurance, dangers teach caution, and encounters broaden their understanding of other peoples. They may acquire new skills without ceasing to be deeply shaped by their original occupation.

This continuity gives the profession a particular identity. A character returning after several years of adventure possesses extraordinary experience, yet often retains the habits, memories, and familiar gestures acquired in youth.

Playing a Layman

The Layman offers the opportunity to create a character whose life was already rich before the campaign began.

A Dorwinadan merchant may have left home to find a missing shipment. A craftswoman from Gondor accompanies travellers in order to repair an ancient structure. A Rohir shepherd seeks several stolen horses, while a Hobbit of the Shire undertakes a journey to bring news to a relative living far from the village.

The character's relationships with family and occupation are essential elements of their history. Who passed on their knowledge? Do they own a house, a workshop, or land to which they hope to return? Does someone still depend upon their work? Is there a promise they wish to honour despite the difficulties ahead?

Their character may be shaped by the habits of their former life. A merchant may be highly confident in negotiations yet struggle to understand the decisions of warriors. A craftsperson may be demanding about the quality of workmanship, while a farmer possesses patience acquired through years of seasonal labour.

The character may also have developed ambitions beyond their trade. A scribe dreams of discovering ancient cities, a boatman longs to sail distant seas, and a servant aspires to lead an independent life.

The profession is particularly suited to campaigns that follow the growth of ordinary people confronted by extraordinary events. It allows special significance to be given to first discoveries, first wounds, and the relationships formed along the road.

Over the course of their life, the Layman will discover that qualities developed in everyday circumstances can prove decisive when trials arise. Their knowledge, loyalty, and the responsibilities they accept will gradually define their place among their companions.

Gamemaster's Notes — The Layman in MERP-RMU

The Layman (Sans Profession) is a non-spell-using, generalist profession, intended for characters whose training does not belong to any specialised adventuring profession.

The Layman has no prime stats.

This feature must be preserved in its entirety in MERP-UI: no stat is automatically designated as prime.

The player is free to choose the stats that reflect the character's origins and personal history.

Choosing an Occupation

An occupation is an essential element of this profession.

Under the historical reference rules, a Layman character chooses an occupation, allowing the Gamemaster to determine which skills are considered professional or commonly used according to the character's work.

Examples include craftspeople, farmers, herders, merchants, ordinary healers, innkeepers, performers, and boatmen.

In MERP-UI, this principle must be applied in accordance with the mechanics actually available. The narrative choice of an occupation does not automatically alter development costs or skill categories. Any additional adaptation must follow the applicable rules or an explicit decision by the Gamemaster.

Magic

The Layman has no professional Base Spell Lists, no favoured realm, and no professional magical specialisation.

Any opportunity to learn spells depends upon the general possibilities of the RMU system and the applicable restrictions. No additional access to magic should be inferred merely from the choice of this profession.

Profession, Occupation, and Culture

The Layman represents a broad orientation of training. The character's occupation defines the knowledge they possess, while their culture determines the traditions, languages, and customs that have shaped their life.

A Rohir farmer, a Khazâd craftsperson, and a Dorwinadan merchant therefore share the same mechanical profession while possessing profoundly different identities.

Finally, this game category should be distinguished from the characters described by Tolkien. Sam Gamgee, Farmer Maggot, and Barliman Butterbur provide remarkable inspiration for the profession, but their literary lives should not be reduced to any particular set of game statistics.

The Layman comes fully into their own when the character has a tangible past, personal relationships, and skills with a genuine purpose in the world. Adventure gradually transforms their experience without erasing the knowledge and attachments that shaped their earlier life.
